title: A telescope built to photograph faraway galaxies has found a comet nobody knew about
excerpt: ESA’s Euclid telescope, designed to map faraway galaxies, caught a comet nobody knew about: C/2026 S1
content:
ESA’s Euclid telescope, designed to map faraway galaxies, caught a comet nobody knew about: C/2026 S1

The European Space Agency’s Euclid telescope was designed to take long, steady pictures of faraway galaxies. Following a new, fast-moving comet isn’t part of its job.

In late September 2026, Euclid caught one anyway, a comet that astronomers didn’t even know about.

Euclid had photographed comets before, but every one of them was already on the books. This is the first comet it has discovered.

Mikko Pöntinen, a Ph.D. student at the University of Helsinki, wrote the software that flagged it. The program was built to pick out small Solar System objects in Euclid’s pictures. Pöntinen worked with the Euclid Consortium group that studies those objects.

“I was excited to see my software flag a ‘streak’ smeared across several images – the result of a fast-moving object,” Pöntinen said.

“By predicting its position I could identify it in other images, in total finding it in five image sets. Further inspection revealed that it had a fuzzy cloud around it, indicative of an active object like a comet that is shedding dust and gas.”

Software flagged a streak

Euclid took the pictures between September 16 and 24, 2026. Over several days, the comet showed up in five different patches of sky. Each patch got two to four pictures, for 16 exposures in all.

One of those exposures ran for more than nine minutes. Because the comet kept moving the whole time, it appeared as a smear of light instead of a dot.

Pöntinen compared the object with lists of known comets and asteroids and found no match. Pöntinen then reported it to the International Astronomical Union’s Minor Planet Center, which collects sightings from observers worldwide.

That report alerted astronomers on the ground, who added their own observations. The center confirmed the comet on October 8. Its official name is C/2026 S1 (Euclid).

The comet orbits high above

C/2026 S1 is about 800 million miles (1.3 billion kilometers) from Earth. That’s roughly the distance from the Sun out to a spot between the orbits of Jupiter and Saturn.

The planets all circle the Sun in roughly one flat plane. This comet doesn’t.

Seen from the Sun, it’s currently about straight up, on a path over the Solar System that takes thousands of years to complete.

Few comets were expected

The band of sky where the planets travel is crowded with comets and asteroids. Euclid stays out of it on purpose, because dust there creates glare that would spoil faint galaxy images.

Euclid also usually photographs each patch of sky only once, a method ESA calls step-and-stare. That means the telescope can’t simply go back for a second look at a comet.

Bruno Altieri, Euclid’s archive scientist, was part of the discovery team. “Very few comets are expected to be discovered by Euclid so it was a happy coincidence that the combination of the comet’s orbit and Euclid’s scanning over those days captured the object in multiple images,” he said.

Over six years, Euclid will record billions of galaxies as far as 10 billion light-years away, to study how dark matter and dark energy shape the universe. One early batch of data alone held more than 26 million galaxies.

Before measuring galaxies, the team has to identify everything in each picture and remove comet trails and stray light. Euclid’s survey stays more than 15 degrees away from the planets’ band.

Even so, a 2025 paper by several members of the same working group estimated that the telescope would record more than 100,000 Solar System objects.

Testing a future comet mission

Comets are icy, dusty leftovers from the birth of the Solar System about 4.6 billion years ago. Most come from the distant Kuiper Belt and Oort Cloud.

Because they’ve changed very little since they formed, scientists study them for clues about where Earth’s water may have come from.

ESA said the quick turnaround, from first sighting to confirmation, shows Euclid can catch new comets while they’re still relatively far from the Sun. That could eventually supply a target for Comet Interceptor, a future ESA mission to visit a comet.

Could C/2026 S1 be that target? Valeria Pettorino, Euclid’s project scientist, had an answer, along with a reason the find still mattered.

“While this particular comet is not a suitable candidate for Comet Interceptor, the process of discovery and alert gives us a real test case for how our two mission teams will coordinate in the future,” Pettorino said.

“And we are of course happy to have discovered a previously unknown comet for the Solar System community to follow-up on.”

Questions still open

ESA hasn’t said why this comet doesn’t suit Comet Interceptor, or how big it is.

The time it takes to complete one orbit is also a rough figure for now, and ESA said astronomers will refine it as more observations of C/2026 S1 come in.

Information from an ESA press release.
